claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy contains significant defect concentrations.
The as-deposited alloy has irregular grain boundaries.
Defects and irregular grain boundaries contribute to a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition.
Annealing near but below the transition temperature can reduce microstructural defects and modify the grain-boundary profile.
Annealing can relieve internal stresses without causing deleterious phase transformations when conducted within an appropriate processing window.
Grain boundaries and defects such as dislocations influence magnetic-domain pinning.
Grain boundaries and defects influence the distribution of energy barriers for the phase transition.
Annealing reduces defect-induced pinning sites and promotes a more uniform grain-boundary distribution.
Reducing pinning and making the grain-boundary distribution more uniform smooths the energy landscape of the magnetostructural transition.
Smoothing the transition energy landscape broadens the transformation and reduces its sharpness and hysteresis.
Annealed samples will show a smoother, less abrupt magnetization change than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will show lower hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Annealing will broaden the magnetocaloric response over a wider temperature range.
The as-deposited baseline has a large but abrupt entropy change and significant hysteresis.
The predictions apply to non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys processed by arc melting or melt spinning.
Large departures in composition, processing, or annealing conditions may produce different magnetocaloric responses.

contradictions.description: The intervention is framed as a post-deposition treatment of an as-deposited material, but the stated applicability boundary instead names arc-melted and melt-spun materials. Arc-melted ingots are not an as-deposited state, so the target processing form and claimed boundary are inconsistent.
